plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks two panels, labeled (a) and (b), each plotting projectile trajectories that leave and return to the same level ground line. In panel (a) three parabolic arcs share one launch point and an angle marked 45 degrees, distinguished by velocity arrows at the origin labeled 30 m/s in orange, 40 m/s in purple, and 50 m/s in teal; a key at the upper right shows y up and x right. Dashed verticals drop from each apex, and three dimension bars beneath the ground line read R = 91.8 m, R = 163 m, and R = 255 m in that same order. Panel (b) instead fixes the speed, labeled v0 = 50 m/s, and varies the angle, with nested arcs at the origin marking 15, 45, and 75 degrees; only two dimension bars appear, R = 128 m ending at a dashed vertical where both the 15-degree and 75-degree curves land, and R = 255 m spanning the 45-degree curve. Matching each color-coded launch arrow to its own range bar isolates one launch parameter at a time. The layout supports the range relationship, in which range grows with the square of initial speed, peaks at 45 degrees, and repeats for complementary angles whose apex heights differ.

interactionPlan.concept: Projectile range on level ground is R = v0² sin(2θ)/g, so at fixed angle range grows with the square of launch speed, while at fixed speed it peaks at 45° and is identical for complementary angles that trade apex height for the same horizontal reach.

interactions.label: Highlight speed (panel a, θ = 45°)
interactions.teaches: With the angle held at 45°, selecting different speeds emphasizes how range scales with v0² — jumping from 30 to 50 m/s more than doubles the range, revealing the quadratic dependence.

interactions.label: Highlight angle (panel b, v0 = 50 m/s)
interactions.teaches: With speed fixed, selecting different angles shows that 45° gives maximum range while complementary angles (15° and 75°) land at the same horizontal distance but reach very different apex heights.

demo_steps.title: All trajectories equally visible
demo_steps.narration: Both panels show all three trajectories at full opacity in their source colors (orange, purple, teal). Each has its own launch arrow, apex guide, and range bar — the complete picture of how speed and angle affect projectile motion.

demo_steps.title: Speed controls range quadratically
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a), the slider highlights the teal (50 m/s) trajectory with a thicker stroke and glow. Compare its range bar (~255 m) to the orange (30 m/s) bar (~92 m) — nearly triple the speed increase yields almost triple the range, because R ∝ v0².

demo_steps.title: 45° gives maximum range
demo_steps.narration: In panel (b), the slider highlights the purple (45°) trajectory. Its range bar (255 m) is the longest — no other angle at this speed can match it.

demo_steps.title: Complementary angles share range, not height
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the orange (15°) arc in panel (b). Notice the teal (75°) arc has an identical range bar value (128 m) yet soars to a much higher apex — same horizontal reach, traded for vertical height.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Range factorizes into a speed term (v0²) and an angle term (sin 2θ): speed sets the overall scale quadratically, while the angle term peaks at 45° and is symmetric about it, so complementary angles always land together but at different heights.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Stack two panels vertically: panel (a) on top, panel (b) below. In each panel, draw ALL three trajectories simultaneously at full opacity with their fixed source colors — orange, purple, teal — as solid curves. Do NOT ghost or fade any trajectory; the default state shows all three equally prominent. The slider interaction adds emphasis (thicker stroke width and a subtle glow or drop-shadow) to the selected trajectory and highlights its corresponding range bar, without dimming the others. Panel (a): three launch arrows at 45° with lengths proportional to 30, 40, 50 m/s, each labeled with its speed value. Panel (b): three launch arrows at 15°, 45°, 75° with equal length (same speed), each labeled with its angle — use at least 11px font for these angle labels. Range bars are double-headed horizontal arrows beneath the ground line with centered 'R ≈ … m' text labels, color-matched to their trajectory. Dashed vertical lines drop from each apex to the ground. The slider snaps to the three discrete values (30/40/50 or 15/45/75) and simply toggles which trajectory gets the emphasis treatment.

authoredContext:
Note particularly that the equation is valid only for launch and impact on a horizontal surface. We see the range is directly proportional to the square of the initial speed v0 and sin2θ0, and it is inversely proportional to the acceleration of gravity. Thus, on the Moon, the range would be six times greater than on Earth for the same initial velocity. Furthermore, we see from the factor sin2θ0 that the range is maximum at 45°. These results are shown in the figure. In (a) we see that the greater the initial velocity, the greater the range. In (b), we see that the range is maximum at 45°. This is true only for conditions neglecting air resistance. If air resistance is considered, the maximum angle is somewhat smaller. It is interesting that the same range is found for two initial launch angles that sum to 90°. The projectile launched with the smaller angle has a lower apex than the higher angle, but they both have the same range.

Trajectories of projectiles on level ground. (a) The greater the initial speed v0, the greater the range for a given initial angle. (b) The effect of initial angle θ0 on the range of a projectile with a given initial speed. Note that the range is the same for initial angles of 15° and 75°, although the maximum heights of those paths are different.

Figure a shows the trajectories of projectiles launched at the same initial 45 degree angle above the horizontal and different initial velocities. The trajectories are shown from launch to landing back at the initial elevation. In orange is the trajectory for 30 meters per second, giving a range R (distance from launch to landing) of 91.8 m. In purple is the trajectory for 40 meters per second, giving a range R of 163 m. In blue is the trajectory for 50 meters per second, giving a range R of 255 m. The maximum height of the projectile increases with initial speed. Figure b shows the trajectories of projectiles launched at the same initial speed of 50 meters per second and different launch angles. The trajectories are shown from launch to landing back at the initial elevation. In orange is the trajectory for an angle of 15 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 128 m. In purple is the trajectory for an angle of 45 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 255 m. In blue is the trajectory for an angle of 75 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 128 m, the same as for the 15 degree trajectory. The maximum height increases with launch angle.

When we speak of the range of a projectile on level ground, we assume R is very small compared with the circumference of Earth. If, however, the range is large, Earth curves away below the projectile and the acceleration resulting from gravity changes direction along the path. The range is larger than predicted by the range equation given earlier because the projectile has farther to fall than it would on level ground, as shown in the figure, which is based on a drawing in Newton’s Principia. If the initial speed is great enough, the projectile goes into orbit. Earth’s surface drops 5 m every 8000 m. In 1 s an object falls 5 m without air resistance. Thus, if an object is given a horizontal velocity of 8000 m/s (or 18,000 mi/hr) near Earth’s surface, it will go into orbit around the planet because the surface continuously falls away from the object. This is roughly the speed of the Space Shuttle in a low Earth orbit when it was operational, or any satellite in a low Earth orbit. These and other aspects of orbital motion, such as Earth’s rotation, are covered in greater depth in Gravitation.

demo_steps.title: Speed controls range quadratically
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a) the angle is locked at 45°. Sweep the speed slider from 30 to 50 m/s and watch the range bar jump from ~92 m to ~255 m — far more than a proportional increase, because R grows with v0 squared.

demo_steps.title: 45° gives maximum range
demo_steps.narration: In panel (b) the speed is locked at 50 m/s. Drag the angle slider toward 45° and the range bar reaches its longest value (255 m); moving to either side of 45° shortens the range symmetrically.

demo_steps.title: Complementary angles share range, not height
demo_steps.narration: Set the angle to 15° and notice the faint 75° complement arc lands at exactly the same x (R = 128 m) yet soars to a much higher apex — same horizontal reach, traded for vertical height.

plan.keyInsight: Range factorizes into a speed term (v0²) and an angle term (sin 2θ): speed sets the overall scale quadratically, while the angle term peaks at 45° and is symmetric about it, so complementary angles always land together but at different heights.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Stack two panels vertically exactly as the source: panel (a) on top, panel (b) below, each with its own ground line and range dimension bars drawn beneath it. Use a consistent color code — orange for the low/steep-shallow reference, purple for the mid, teal for the high/steep reference — and let the single live arc in each panel take the color nearest its current parameter value. Draw launch arrows from the origin with arrowheads and italic speed/angle labels; mark the 45° (panel a) and 15/45/75° (panel b) angle arcs at the origin. Dashed verticals drop from each apex to the ground. Range bars are double-headed horizontal arrows with centered 'R = … m' labels. In panel (b), when the angle slider is away from 45°, render the complement (90° − θ) as a thin dashed arc of the same landing x to make the symmetry visible. Keep ghost reference arcs low-opacity so the live slider-driven arc and its range bar dominate. Orientation key (y up, x right) sits at the top-right of panel (a).

interactions.label: Highlight speed (panel a, θ = 45°)
interactions.teaches: With the angle held at 45°, selecting different speeds emphasizes how range scales with v0² — jumping from 30 to 50 m/s more than doubles the range, revealing the quadratic dependence.

interactions.label: Highlight angle (panel b, v0 = 50 m/s)
interactions.teaches: With speed fixed, selecting different angles shows that 45° gives maximum range while complementary angles (15° and 75°) land at the same horizontal distance but reach very different apex heights.

demo_steps.title: All trajectories equally visible
demo_steps.narration: Both panels show all three trajectories at full opacity in their source colors (orange, purple, teal). Each has its own launch arrow, apex guide, and range bar — the complete picture of how speed and angle affect projectile motion.

demo_steps.title: Speed controls range quadratically
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a), the slider highlights the teal (50 m/s) trajectory with a thicker stroke and glow. Compare its range bar (~255 m) to the orange (30 m/s) bar (~92 m) — nearly triple the speed increase yields almost triple the range, because R ∝ v0².

demo_steps.title: 45° gives maximum range
demo_steps.narration: In panel (b), the slider highlights the purple (45°) trajectory. Its range bar (255 m) is the longest — no other angle at this speed can match it.

demo_steps.title: Complementary angles share range, not height
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the orange (15°) arc in panel (b). Notice the teal (75°) arc has an identical range bar value (128 m) yet soars to a much higher apex — same horizontal reach, traded for vertical height.

plan.keyInsight: Range factorizes into a speed term (v0²) and an angle term (sin 2θ): speed sets the overall scale quadratically, while the angle term peaks at 45° and is symmetric about it, so complementary angles always land together but at different heights.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Stack two panels vertically: panel (a) on top, panel (b) below. In each panel, draw ALL three trajectories simultaneously at full opacity with their fixed source colors — orange, purple, teal — as solid curves. Do NOT ghost or fade any trajectory; the default state shows all three equally prominent. The slider interaction adds emphasis (thicker stroke width and a subtle glow or drop-shadow) to the selected trajectory and highlights its corresponding range bar, without dimming the others. Panel (a): three launch arrows at 45° with lengths proportional to 30, 40, 50 m/s, each labeled with its speed value. Panel (b): three launch arrows at 15°, 45°, 75° with equal length (same speed), each labeled with its angle — use at least 11px font for these angle labels. Range bars are double-headed horizontal arrows beneath the ground line with centered 'R ≈ … m' text labels, color-matched to their trajectory. Dashed vertical lines drop from each apex to the ground. The slider snaps to the three discrete values (30/40/50 or 15/45/75) and simply toggles which trajectory gets the emphasis treatment.
